did_you_know.text: Did you know? At the beginning of the chapter, the restoration of Israel is described: the LORD will have compassion on Jacob, choose Israel again, and settle them in their own land. Foreigners will also be able to join the house of Jacob.
Did you know? The chapter describes a reversal of power: the nations will bring Israel back to its land, and the Israelites will rule over those who enslaved them.
Did you know? After describing Israel’s rest, the prophet presents a taunt against the king of Babylon and uses it to describe the breaking of his rule: “How the oppressor has ceased!”
Did you know? The ruler’s downfall is portrayed as bringing rest to the whole earth, so that the quiet land is described as breaking into joyful singing.
Did you know? Sheol is vividly portrayed as awakening to welcome the king of Babylon and rousing the kings of the past from their resting places.

Did you know? The phrase “Morning Star, son of Dawn” appears in the description of the ruler’s fall from heaven to earth; later in the chapter, it becomes clear that this is an image of pride and downfall.
Did you know? The king of Babylon is portrayed as saying in his heart that he would ascend to heaven, raise his throne, and make himself like the Most High—an ambition expressing his extreme pride.
Did you know? After his fall, onlookers wonder whether this is the same man who shook kingdoms, destroyed cities, and did not release his prisoners.
Did you know? In the middle of the chapter, the LORD swears that his plan will be fulfilled; later, it is said that he will break Assyria and remove its yoke from his people.

Did you know? The chapter ends by contrasting the defeat of the Philistines with the security of Zion: when asked what answer should be given to the messengers of the nation, the response is that the LORD has founded Zion, and in her the poor of his people find refuge.
